new_statements.quote: Word stress is on the penultimate syllable of multisyllabic roots. This is much the same as Galela (Shelden 1989), but different from Loloda and Tobelo (van Baarda 1904:356-9) and Tabaru, where stress can occur on the antepenultimate or penultimate syllable depending on affixation (Kotynski 1988:156). This is also much different than Sahu, where the stress is phonemic (Visser and Voorhoeve 1987:19). Tidore stress is as follows: (3) ane ['ane] 'forehead' gumi ['gumi] 'moustache' dofolo [do'folo] 'head'. There are several words in Tidore which at first glance sound as if they have ultimate stress, but when listened to in slow speech the last vowel appears to be lengthened (see discussion on geminate vowels, Sec. 3.2.7).
new_statements.citation: Pikkert, Joost J. J. & Cheryl M. Pikkert. 1995. A first look at Tidore phonology. In Wyn D. Laidig (ed.), Descriptive studies in languages of Maluku, part II (NUSA 38), 43-70. Jakarta: Universitas Katolik Indonesia Atma Jaya.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic roots (['ane], ['gumi], [do'folo]). Words that sound final-stressed have a lengthened final vowel which the authors analyse as a sequence of two vowels (kare [ka'ree], mafu [ma'fuu]), so stress remains penultimate under that analysis; sec. 3.2.7 (p. 56) states this VV analysis 'is compatible with the generalized stress rule... an otherwise highly regular penultimate stress rule'. Stress is not contrastive (contrasted explicitly with Sahu, 'where the stress is phonemic').
new_statements.exceptions: Endnote 2 (p. 68): 'Some exceptions to the penultimate stress rule are as follows: a. words formed by reduplication of monosyllabic roots (e.g. dum-dum "bathroom") b. compound words with a monosyllabic second constituent such as enage from ena "it" plus ge "this", and jibobomoi from jibobo "spoon" plus moi "one".' Also the final-lengthened-vowel words (kare [ka'ree] 'here', kata [ka'taa] 'there', mafu [ma'fuu] 'to sell', hali [ha'lii] 'family', kombo [kom'boo] 'little'), phonemically written with an accent mark in the orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, on roots (isolated citation forms from a c. 2500-word lexicon); the rule is stated for roots, and stress under affixation is not discussed. Data from the Soa Sio dialect (villages Soa Sio, Gura Bunga, Gamtufkange, Tidore island), 1993-94.
new_statements.identity_note: Pikkert & Pikkert 1995 describe the Soa Sio dialect of Tidore island (villages Soa Sio, Gura Bunga, Gamtufkange); they state the Mareku dialect differs only in occasional vowel choice and a word-final front high vowel and is mutually intelligible. Same language as tido1248; no separate glottocode for the dialect.

sources.locator: sec. 3.1 'Word Stress', p. 46 (PDF p. 4); exceptions in endnote 2, p. 68 (PDF p. 26); sec. 3.2.7, pp. 55-56
sources.note: Sec. 3.1 Word Stress (p. 46): word stress on the penultimate syllable of multisyllabic roots, examples ['ane], ['gumi], [do'folo]; apparent final stress is a lengthened final vowel analysed as a VV sequence ([ka'ree] 'here'), so still penultimate; endnote 2 (p. 68) lists exceptions (reduplicated monosyllabic roots dum-dum; compounds with monosyllabic second member enage, jibobomoi); sec. 3.2.7 says the VV analysis is 'compatible with the generalized stress rule... an otherwise highly regular penultimate stress rule'. Data = Soa Sio dialect, villages Soa Sio, Gura Bunga, Gamtufkange, 1993-94.
